routes.description: Establish that moral understanding depends on evolved, story-shaped interpretive structures and that religious narratives and God-language can preserve, embody, and transmit deep moral universals while remaining subject to truthful correction.
routes.successCriteria: Connect moral intuition to narrative mediation, supply a disciplined account of biblical interpretation and God-language, and explain why preserving developmentally inherited religious wisdom contributes something that abstract factual inquiry alone cannot replace.

motionBridge.description: Show that religious stories, God-language, and biblical tradition can ground moral truth and meaning through enduring interpretive structures rather than merely fixed supernatural assertions.

centralBridges.description: Establish that facts and values are accessed through prior intuitions and evolved interpretive structures that stories can embody.
Explain how developmental and psychological interpretation can recover durable moral meaning while subordinating isolated dogmatic claims to truthful knowledge-updating.
Show that cross-cultural variation can coexist with deep moral and narrative universals constrained by consilience across independent domains.
Demonstrate why inherited religious forms remain materially useful for embodying and transmitting wisdom that helped generate modern rational inquiry.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish the dangers of evidence-resistant fundamentalism from religion as such and identify truthful discourse as a corrective process.
Provide concrete mechanisms by which religious concepts and practices can orient conscience, reflection, repair, and embodied conduct.

routes.description: Establish an objective moral foundation in the conditions of conscious beings and show that revisable, evidence-responsive inquiry can retain valid psychological and ethical insights without dependence on revelation, inherited dogma, or ambiguous God-language.
routes.successCriteria: Ground moral truth without sectarian premises, identify the epistemic and moral liabilities of scriptural authority and flexible reinterpretation, and show that open causal inquiry provides a clearer and more adaptable basis for moral correction.

motionBridge.description: Show that moral realism, well-being, and continuously revisable inquiry can ground truth and meaning more directly than dogmatic or ambiguously reinterpreted religious frameworks.

centralBridges.description: Establish conscious well-being and the avoidance of universal misery as an objective foundation broad enough to include intentions, character, and social relations.
Explain how revelation and evidence-resistant doctrine preserve harmful commands and obstruct correction even when tribal aggression has deeper evolutionary roots.
Show that metaphorical reinterpretation, religious diversity, and semantic revision prevent scripture or God-language from supplying distinctive moral knowledge.
Demonstrate that inquiry into actual causal variables can preserve valid concerns while improving on fixed heuristics inherited from ancient conditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate genuine transformative experiences from culturally contingent doctrines so that spirituality does not validate sectarian claims.
Account for how ambiguous religious language can lend support to conventional supernatural commitments beyond the abstract meanings being defended.

sections.title: Foundations of Moral Truth and Value
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether conscious well-being supplies an irreducible objective basis for morality or whether value judgments necessarily depend on evolved intuitions and story-shaped interpretive structures.

sections.title: Scriptural Authority and Interpretive Constraint
sections.rationale: This issue bears on whether developmental and psychological readings can recover authoritative moral wisdom from biblical tradition or whether literal harms and flexible reinterpretation defeat that claim.

sections.title: God-Language, Meaning, and Moral Practice
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether abstract and pragmatic accounts of God, prayer, conscience, and truthful embodiment clarify a genuine moral reality or create semantic ambiguity about conventional religious commitments.

sections.title: Dogmatism, Harm, and Corrective Inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue addresses the causal role of religious doctrine in violence and moral error, the broader roots of fundamentalism, and the capacity of open discourse and evidence-responsive inquiry to correct inherited beliefs.

sections.title: Moral Universals, Religious Diversity, and Inherited Wisdom
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether recurring structures across traditions support deep universals and justify preserving inherited wisdom, or whether disagreement and changing conditions favor nonsectarian causal explanation.
